title: CSU researchers celebrate construction milestone in Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) project
excerpt: The major construction milestone marks a new phase for one of the world's most ambitious physics experiments.
content:
Colorado State University researchers are celebrating a major construction milestone in the international Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) project, marking a new phase for one of the world’s most ambitious physics experiments.

DUNE is a leading-edge, international experiment for neutrino science that aims to further research into several fundamental questions about the nature of matter and the evolution of the universe. It centers on two massive detectors placed on either end of an intense neutrino beam. One detector will record particle interactions near the source of the beam at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Illinois, while another, buried deep underground, will collect measurements on the other end in South Dakota. Construction on this second facility began last week according to a release by Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory.

The project involves more than 1,500 collaborators from over 200 institutions in over 35 countries, including the European Organization for Nuclear Research. CSU is a founding member on the project, and several faculty in the Department of Physics lead work in detector development, computing and governance as well as theoretical neutrino research within it.

CSU Professor Robert Wilson has held several leadership roles within DUNE since 2003.

“DUNE has been a cornerstone of CSU’s particle physics program for more than two decades,” Wilson said. “We’re excited to continue collaborating with international partners as the project moves closer to detector installation and scientific discovery.”

The underground detector space in South Dakota is planned to be completed by 2029 with the entire apparatus slated to finish in 2030.
